title-group.article-title: Ethnobotanical Uses, Perceived Availability and Implications for the Conservation of Pavetta crassipes K. Schum. in Benin

abstract.p: Medicinal plants are central to rural health systems and livelihoods in sub-Saharan Africa, yet increasing exploitation threatens their persistence. Pavetta crassipes K. Schum., a shrub widely used in West African savannas, provides remedies for numerous ailments but remains poorly documented in Benin. This study aimed to fill that gap by documenting local knowledge, uses, and conservation perspectives of Pavetta crassipes across all twelve departments of Benin. Data were collected through structured interviews with 582 households and 87 herbal tea sellers, focusing on plant parts used, therapeutic applications, availability, and management strategies. Respondents reported its use in the treatment of about 43 diseases, with leaves being the most frequently cited organ (84.2%). Despite its cultural and medicinal importance, respondents reported declining availability due to bushfires (24%) and leaf marketing (20%), followed by climate change (17%), leaf collection (13%), and tree felling (11%). Conservation strategies mentioned by local communities included planting (26%) and restricting destructive harvesting practices (21%). These findings highlight the dual role of Pavetta crassipes as both a critical health resource and a vulnerable species facing anthropogenic pressures. This study establishes a baseline ethnobotanical database and highlights the need to integrate local practices into conservation planning to secure the future of medicinal plant resources.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Medicinal plants play a crucial role in sustaining livelihoods and healthcare systems worldwide, providing employment and income to millions of people in both developing and industrialized countries [1,2,3]. Beyond their therapeutic and cultural importance, they contribute significantly to the global economy, with products valued at approximately US$400 billion and expanding at an annual rate of 15–25% [4]. The global herbal medicine market was valued at $51 billion in 2017 and is projected to reach nearly $5 trillion by 2050 [5,6]. In Africa, where modern healthcare services are often inaccessible or unaffordable, wild medicinal plants remain an essential part of primary healthcare, especially in rural areas, while also contributing to household income and food security [7,8]. However, the heavy reliance on wild-harvested plants, combined with seasonal availability, habitat transformation and increasing market demand, may increase harvesting pressure on some species and raise concerns about their long-term availability and sustainable management [9,10,11].

One species of particular importance is Pavetta crassipes K. Schum. [12], a shrub native to Africa. Its geographical range extends across West, Central, East and parts of southern Africa, including Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Ghana, Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Mali, Nigeria, Senegal, Togo, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique and Zambia. The species occurs primarily in seasonally dry tropical environments and is associated with savannas, wooded grasslands, woodland formations and forest margins. At the global level, P. crassipes is currently classified as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. However, this global assessment does not necessarily describe local patterns of availability or the effects of harvesting and habitat transformation on particular populations. In Benin, the species is known for its medicinal and other ethnobotanical uses, including treatments reported for malaria and other health conditions. Pharmacological studies have also investigated the biological activity of extracts from the species. Its leaves are consumed as vegetables or used to treat ailments such as fever, schistosomiasis, convulsions, pain, hookworm infection, mental illness, and microbial diseases [13,14]. Pharmacological studies further highlight its medicinal potential: alkaloid extracts display antimalarial activity [15], while ethanol extracts reduce blood pressure in animal models [16]. These multiple uses, combined with its availability in local markets, make Pavetta crassipes one of the most valued medicinal plants in West Africa [12]. Although Pavetta crassipes has been widely documented in traditional medicine and its extracts have demonstrated pharmacological activities in experimental studies, we found no reliable evidence of an officially approved pharmaceutical preparation specifically containing the species or its derivatives. Experimental work has nevertheless explored the formulation of herbal products containing P. crassipes extracts, including herbal lozenges evaluated for cough suppression, indicating potential for future pharmaceutical development rather than current official medicinal recognition [17]. However, ethnobotanical use alone does not demonstrate population decline, and the extent to which harvesting and habitat transformation affect wild populations of P. crassipes remains insufficiently documented.

Although Pavetta crassipes has been reported in ethnobotanical and medicinal plant studies in Benin and other West African countries [18], existing information is largely derived from local or market-based surveys and broader inventories of medicinal plants in which the species represents only one component of the recorded flora [19,20,21]. Consequently, available knowledge remains fragmented with respect to geographical variation in reported uses, plant parts harvested, perceived availability, reported threats and conservation perspectives across Benin. In addition, few studies have examined these dimensions simultaneously at a national scale. A geographically broad assessment is therefore needed to better understand how knowledge and perceptions surrounding P. crassipes vary across ecological and socio-cultural contexts and to identify priorities for future ecological and conservation research.

This study addresses these knowledge gaps by documenting local and local knowledge, reported uses and perceptions of Pavetta crassipes across Benin’s twelve departments. Specifically, the study aimed to: (i) document the diversity of reported uses and plant parts harvested; (ii) assess respondents’ perceptions of the species’ local availability, habitats and threats; and (iii) document reported and proposed conservation measures. We further examined whether ethnobotanical uses and perceptions varied among socio-demographic and geographical groups. We expected that patterns of use and perceptions would vary across socio-cultural and ecological contexts because differences in cultural practices, resource accessibility and environmental conditions may influence human interactions with the species.

sec.title: 2.1. Study Area
sec.p: This study was conducted in the Republic of Benin, a West African country located between latitudes 6°10′ and 12°25′ N and longitudes 0°45′ and 3°55′ E. Benin is divided into twelve departments and spans three major climatic zones the humid Guineo-Congolian zone in the south, the sub-humid Sudano-Guinean transition zone in the center, and the drier Sudanian zone in the north. This ecological gradient strongly influences vegetation types, ranging from dense semi-deciduous forests and savanna mosaics to dry woodlands, which together harbor diverse populations of Pavetta crassipes K. Schum. (Figure 1). Recent spatial distribution research conducted in Benin indicates that P. crassipes occurs across the country’s three major climatic zones, with important ecological associations in Sudanian and Sudano-Guinean savanna environments, while suitable habitats and occurrence records are also found within the Guinean zone. The distribution of the species is influenced by climatic and environmental conditions, including temperature, precipitation, soil characteristics and land use. These findings suggest that populations occurring across Benin may experience different ecological conditions and anthropogenic pressures. Beyond its ecological range, the cultural and economic importance of this non-timber forest product (NTFP) extends across ethnic and religious communities. The surveys were conducted in the major markets of each department, which also function as territorial centers of the country’s main socio-cultural groups (Figure 2).

The national coverage of this study was intended to capture variation across Benin’s major ecological and socio-cultural contexts. For analytical purposes, the twelve departments were grouped within the three major climatic zones of Benin, the Guineo-Congolian zone in the south, the Sudano-Guinean transition zone in the center, and the Sudanian zone in the north. The geographical distribution of survey sites and respondents across departments and climatic zones is presented in Figure 2.

sec.title: 2.2. Site Selection and Data Collection
sec.p: A preliminary survey was conducted across Benin’s 12 departments to identify localities and markets where Pavetta crassipes was known, used or traded. Potential survey sites were identified through consultations with community leaders, local resource persons, traders and traditional herbal practitioners. Based on this preliminary assessment, data were subsequently collected in 102 rural communities and major markets distributed across the country. Site selection was therefore purposive rather than based on a random national sampling design. Accordingly, the resulting findings should be interpreted as reflecting the knowledge, uses and perceptions of respondents from communities and markets where P. crassipes was known, used or commercialized, rather than as unbiased estimate representative of the entire population of Benin.

Two categories of respondents were included: (i) household respondents representing local users and holders of ethnobotanical knowledge (582) and (ii) herbal tea sellers (87) representing actors involved in the commercialization and transmission of knowledge related to medicinal plants (Supplementary Materials Table S1). The respondents encompassed major sociolinguistic groups in Benin, including Fon, Adja, Yoruba, Bariba, and Dendi communities, all of which have longstanding traditions of plant-based healing [22]. In rural communities, traditional healers and older farmers were particularly important, as source of ethnobotanical information because medicinal plants knowledge is predominantly transmitted orally across generations and embedded in both traditional practices and everyday healthcare. In total, 582 household respondents and 87 herbal tea sellers were interviewed using a standardized questionnaire adapted from [23]. The questionnaire was adapted to the local socio-cultural context and pilot-tested before the main survey. It collected information on the plant parts used, frequency and types of use, availability, habitats, perceived threats, and suggested conservation measures, thereby integrating quantitative data with qualitative insights. Interviews were conducted in languages familiar to respondents by trained interviewers, and responses were systematically coded into predefined categories for ailments and use types. Multiple responses were retained and treated as separate use reports where applicable. To minimize recall and interviewer bias, respondents were asked standardized questions, interviewers followed a common protocol, and plant specimens or vernacular names were used, where possible, to facilitate accurate recall and species identification.

The research protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee for Scientific Research of the University of Parakou, Benin, during its ordinary session held on 13 November 2025. Ethical authorization was formally granted on 29 December 2025 (Certificate No. 582-2025/UP/R/VR-RU/SA). The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles and applicable national and institutional regulations governing research involving human participants. Prior to data collection, all participants provided free, informed, and written consent after receiving information about the study’s objectives, the voluntary nature of their participation, and their right to decline any question or withdraw at any time without consequence. Confidentiality was maintained throughout the research process, and collected data were anonymized to protect participants’ identities. The relevant local authorities were also informed about the research objectives and granted permission to conduct fieldwork in the participating communities.

sec.title: 2.3. Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Ethnobotanical knowledge and perception of Pavetta crassipes were analyzed using the use value (UV) index, calculated as the number of uses cited per respondent (Supplementary Materials Table S2) divided by total respondents [24].UV=∑I=1InUi/n where Ui is the number of uses cited by respondent i and n is the total number of respondents.

Because the number of uses cited per respondent (Ui) is a count data, we modeled the effect of socio-demographics parameters on it using a generalized linear model (GLM) with a Poisson distribution and a log link. All 669 respondents had complete data for these variables. Overdispersion was assessed by comparing the Pearson dispersion ratio to 1 (check_overdispersion(), package performance) [25]; none was detected (dispersion ratio = 0.032, χ2(662) = 21.29, p = 1.000), so the Poisson model was retained rather than a negative-binomial alternative. Model assumptions and goodness-of-fit were verified using simulated residuals (simulateResiduals(), package DHARMa [26], 1000 simulations), and the overall contribution of each predictor was tested with type II likelihood-ratio tests (Anova(), package car). The significance threshold was set at α = 0.05 throughout.

A binomial GLM with a logit link was used to test whether the perceived cultural or economic importance of the species (binary outcome: important vs. not important) was associated with age class (young [reference], adult, old; derived from continuous age using cut-points at 29 and 59 years), sex (reference: female) and education level (reference: no formal education), with no interaction terms (n = 669, no missing data). Odds ratios and 95% profile-likelihood confidence intervals were obtained by exponentiating model coefficients (tidy(), package broom [27], conf.method = “profile”). Overall model fit was evaluated with a likelihood-ratio test against the null (intercept-only) model, McFadden’s and Nagelkerke’s pseudo-R2, and Akaike’s Information Criterion; multicollinearity was checked with the generalized variance inflation factor (vif(), package car), and assumptions were verified with simulated residuals (DHARMa). As for the UV model, the overall contribution of each predictor was tested with type II likelihood-ratio tests, and the significance threshold was set at α = 0.05.
Perceived threats were quantified using the Relative Frequency of Citation (RFC):RFC=nN×100 where n is the number of respondents citing a given threat and N is the total sample size.

To explore how perceived threats relate to socio-demographic groups, respondents were categorized according the gender, age groups (young, adult, old), and education level (no formal education, primary, secondary, university).

The association between the reported form of use (medicinal, food, firewood, magical, plant brush) and, respectively, gender, education level and age class was tested with Pearson’s chi-squared tests of independence with the functionnchisq.test() from the package stats on the corresponding contingency tables. Because a given respondent could report more than one form of use, these tests were conducted at the level of individual use-citations rather than respondents (n = 688 citations). Effect sizes were quantified with bias-corrected Cramér’s V, with the package rcompanion [28]; where the omnibus test was significant, adjusted standardized residuals were examined to identify the cells driving the association, and pairwise comparisons between forms of use were performed with chi-squared tests corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (pairwiseNominalIndependence(), package rcompanion).

To examine how the perception of threats varied across socio-demographic profiles, a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed using the function PCA() form the package FactoMineR [29], on the correlation matrix and on a table crossing the six reported threat categories (tree felling, fuelwood collection, climate change, leaf collection, fruit collection and bark collection) with the 17 non-empty socio-demographic subgroups defined by the combination of sex, education level and age class (Supplementary Materials Tables S3 and S4). The first two components were retained for interpretation, and the quality of representation of each subgroup on these components was assessed using squared cosine (cos2) values. All analyses were performed in the statistical software R, version 4.4.1 [30].

sec.title: 3.1. Socio-Demographic Characteristics Do Not Determine Knowledge of Pavetta crassipes Uses
sec.p: We observed that socio-demographic characteristics including, age (IRR = 1.00, 95% CI [0.99, 1.00], p = 0.860; Table 1) and gender (IRR = 1.01, 95% CI [0.86, 1.18], p = 0.918; Table 1) were not significantly associated with the number of uses cited. However, educational level was associated with the number of uses cited for Pavetta crassipes. Thus, relative to no formal education respondents, none of the education levels differed significantly in the number of uses cited, including literate (IRR = 0.97, 95% CI [0.74, 1.26], p = 0.838; Table 1), primary (IRR = 0.99, 95% CI [0.81, 1.21], p = 0.923; Table 1), secondary (IRR = 1.02, 95% CI [0.83, 1.26], p = 0.844; Table 1) and university education (IRR = 0.97, 95% CI [0.64, 1.42], p = 0.869; Table 1). These results suggest that the overall knowledge and reported use of the species may be relatively widespread across the socio-demographic groups represented in the study.

sec.title: 3.2. Patterns of Use Vary Across Social Categories Despite Overall Medicinal Dominance
sec.p: Although socio-demographic traits of respondents were not associated to the overall number of uses cited, the reported form of use was significantly associated with gender (χ2 = 9.88, p = 0.043, Cramér’s V = 0.09), education level (χ2 = 48.78, p < 0.001, Cramér’s V = 0.11) and age class (χ2 = 24.02, p = 0.002, Cramér’s V = 0.11), which strongly influenced how Pavetta crassipes was used (Figure 3). Thus, men reported a broader diversity of uses (food, firewood, magical practices, brush material) compared to women, who focused more on medicinal purposes (Figure 3a). Similarly, respondents with higher education mentioned more diversified non-medicinal uses (Figure 3b). Across age groups, adults frequently reported medicinal use, whereas young and old respondents were more likely to mention non-medicinal uses such as firewood or ritual practices, with magical practices being especially frequent among elders (Figure 3c). Standardized residual analysis confirmed that medicinal use was cited more often than expected among women (adjusted residual = 2.75) and magical use more often than expected among men (adjusted residual = 2.93); pairwise comparisons showed that magical and medicinal uses differed most strongly between gender (adjusted p = 0.031, Benjamini–Hochberg-corrected). Adults cited medicinal use more often than expected (adjusted residual = 2.87), whereas magical practices were especially frequent among elders (adjusted residual = 3.89). Because a respondent could report more than one form of use, these analyses were conducted at the level of individual use-citations (n = 688) rather than respondents (n = 669).

sec.title: 3.3. Perceived Cultural and Economic Importance of Pavetta crassipes Is Only Weakly Associated with Education Level
sec.p: The perceived cultural or economic importance of Pavetta crassipes was not strongly associated with by respondents’ socio-demographic profile overall (binomial GLM: residual deviance = 258.47 on 661 df, null deviance = 268.84 on 668 df, AIC = 274.47; likelihood-ratio test of the full model against the null model: χ2(7) = 10.38, p = 0.168; McFadden’s pseudo-R2 = 0.039, Nagelkerke’s pseudo-R2 = 0.047, Table 2). Type II likelihood-ratio tests indicated no significant overall effect of age class (χ2(2) = 1.66, p = 0.436) or sex (χ2(1) = 0.10, p = 0.754), while education level approached significance (χ2(4) = 9.39, p = 0.052). At the level of individual categories, relative to respondents with no formal education, those with secondary education were significantly less likely to consider the species culturally or economically important (OR = 0.28, 95% CI [0.09, 0.74], p = 0.014; Table 2), whereas literate (OR = 0.44, 95% CI [0.13, 1.57], p = 0.186), primary (OR = 0.89, 95% CI [0.27, 2.98], p = 0.847; Table 2) and university-educated respondents (OR = 0.79, 95% CI [0.12, 15.5], p = 0.834; Table 2) did not differ significantly from respondents with no formal education. Age class (adult: OR = 1.18, 95% CI [0.27, 3.67], p = 0.798; old: OR = 0.68, 95% CI [0.14, 2.48], p = 0.587; Table 2) and sex (male: OR = 1.12, 95% CI [0.54, 2.30], p = 0.753; Table 2) were not significantly associated with perceived importance.

Regarding perceived threats, households primarily identified hunting (29.42%) and agriculture (24.76%), whereas vendors most frequently cited transhumance (24.82%) and hunting (24.08%); plantation was rarely perceived as a threat by either group (Figure 4).

sec.title: 3.4. Leaves as the Primary Organ Used of Pavetta crassipes
sec.p: Leaves were the most frequently cited plant part of Pavetta crassipes all the pool of surveyed respondents (84.2%), whereas the whole plant (8.42%), fruits (4.35%), branches (1.45%), roots (0.87%), trunk (0.43%) and bark (0.29%) were less frequently reported (Figure 4a). Respondents reported variation in perceived availability, with 54% indicating seasonal limitations in access and 46% reporting year-round availability (Figure 4b). The species was reported to be used in the treatment of 43 health conditions, with malaria being the most frequently cited condition (Supplementary Materials Table S2). Remedies relied predominantly on leaves (88%), typically prepared as decoctions (70%) and, in some cases, combined with other plant species. The use value of Pavetta crassipes varied across ecological zone and socio-demographic groups (Figure 5), with higher values in the Sudanian zone, among men, farmers, and older/adult respondents, and lowest in the Guinean zone, among women, artisans, and young people. Wide error bars for breeders and young respondents indicate more variable knowledge/use within those groups, while farmers and older people show more consistent, higher familiarity with the species (Figure 6). These patterns suggest that gender, age, and respondent’s profession may influence knowledge and recognition of the species’ uses including the agroecological zone of the respondent place of leaving.

sec.title: 3.5. Habitat Use and Perceived Threats to Pavetta crassipes Populations
sec.p: Respondents identified fields (31.7%) and forests (20.1%) as the main habitats where they encountered Pavetta crassipes, followed by fallows (14.4%), gallery forests (7.5%), rocky soils (6.8%) and residential areas (5.2%). Savanna habitats were less frequently mentioned (2.7%), while 11.7% of respondents did not identify a specific habitat (Figure 6a). Perceptions of the relative occurrence of developmental stages suggested that respondents encountered semi-mature individuals more frequently than seedlings, young individuals or mature individuals (Figure 6b). However, because these observations were based on respondents’ perceptions rather than standardized ecological inventories, they should not be interpreted as direct estimates of population structure, recruitment or demographic decline. Regarding perceived threats, households primarily identified hunting (29.42%) and agriculture (24.76%), whereas vendors most frequently cited transhumance (24.82%) and hunting (24.08%); plantation was rarely perceived as a threat by either group (Figure 7). Respondents identified multiple threats, with bushfires (24%) and leaf marketing (20%) considered most critical, followed by climate change (17%), leaf collection (13%), and tree felling (11%). Other pressures, including fuelwood, fruit, logging, or bark harvesting, were mentioned by fewer than 5% (Figure 8a). While some threats (e.g., bush fire, climate change) exhibit reasonably consistent geographic clustering between department and commune scales, others are highly commune-specific, meaning department-level averages can mask local variation in perceived threats (Supplementary Materials Figures S1 and S2).

The principal component analysis performed on the citation profiles of six threat categories across socio-demographic subgroups showed that the first two components jointly explained 74.3% of the variance (PC1 = 48.8%, PC2 = 25.5%; Figure 8b and Supplementary Materials Table S2). PC1 was most strongly correlated with tree felling (r = 0.95) and leaf collection (r = 0.91) and was best represented among adult men with secondary education and elderly women with primary education (cos2 = 0.91 and 0.90, respectively). PC2 was most strongly correlated with bark collection (r = 0.76) and fruit collection (r = 0.71) and was best represented among illiterate adult men and no formal education elderly men (cos2 = 0.81 and 0.65, respectively) (Figure 8b). Conservation strategies most frequently proposed included planting Pavetta crassipes (26%), avoiding systematic logging (21%), and promoting general protection measures (13%) (Figure 9). Others suggested improved collection techniques (7%), bushfire control (6%), targeted conservation (4%), and awareness campaigns (2%). Importantly, 23% reported knowing no conservation options, reflecting gaps in management awareness (Figure 9).

sec.title: 4.1. Cultural and Medicinal Importance of Pavetta crassipes Reflects Widespread Ethnobotanical Knowledge
sec.p: Our findings reveal that knowledge of Pavetta crassipes is widely shared across age, gender, and education categories, underscoring its cultural salience. This supports the common knowledge hypothesis, which posits that highly valued plants are broadly recognized within communities [24,31]. Leaves were the most frequently cited plant part, consistent with accessibility theories in ethnomedicine, where renewable organs are preferred over destructive harvesting of roots or bark [32,33]. Medicinal applications dominated, with malaria the most frequently reported ailment, aligning with findings for other culturally important plants in West Africa [34,35]. The documentation of 43 reported health conditions illustrates the broad ethnomedicinal importance attributed to the species by respondents. These reported uses should not, however, be interpreted as direct evidence of clinical efficacy, although some pharmacological studies have investigated the biological activity of extracts from P. crassipes. Beyond medicine, diversified uses were reported, including food, firewood, and magical practices, especially by men and elders. This multifunctionality may increase the diversity of ways in which the species is harvested and used, although the present study did not quantify total harvesting intensity [36].

sec.title: 4.2. Local Ecological Knowledge Highlights Habitat Specificity and Regeneration Challenges
sec.p: Respondents identified fields and forests as the principal habitats where Pavetta crassipes was encountered and reported differences in the perceived occurrence of individuals at different developmental stages. These observations provide useful local ecological knowledge but should not be interpreted as direct evidence of population decline, recruitment limitation or changes in population structure because no standardized ecological inventory or demographic assessment was conducted. Perceptions of local scarcity may reflect several factors, including accessibility, habitat transformation, changes in harvesting locations or actual changes in abundance. This reflects the resource depletion hypothesis, whereby plants exploited in agricultural mosaics regenerate poorly compared to those in intact ecosystems [37]. Although semi-mature individuals remain relatively common, recruitment bottlenecks threaten long-term population viability. Similar regeneration constraints have been documented where leaf harvesting and land-use change limit recovery of medicinal species [38,39]. Future ecological studies should therefore quantify population density, size-class structure, regeneration and habitat conditions across the species’ range in Benin. Bushfires, leaf commercialization and harvesting practices were among the most frequently reported pressures. However, the relative frequency with which respondents cited these factors does not measure their actual ecological impact. Their effects on P. crassipes populations require direct evaluation through ecological studies combining information on harvesting intensity, fire regimes, land-use change and population performance. Fire pressure mirrors broader findings that recurrent burns suppress woody plant recruitment in savannas [40]. Meanwhile, commercialization highlights the role of market demand in accelerating extinction risks of culturally important species [41]. Socio-demographic variation in threat perception further underscores that ecological knowledge is socially differentiated.

sec.title: 4.3. Domestication and Community-Based Strategies Are Promising Pathways for Conservation
sec.p: Respondents proposed conservation strategies such as planting and avoiding systematic logging, reflecting awareness of the need for management. These align with the domestication pathway hypothesis, suggesting that cultivation reduces pressure on wild populations while preserving cultural and economic value [42]. Incorporation of Pavetta crassipes into agroforestry systems, as done for other medicinal species [43,44], could provide a sustainable alternative. However, the fact that nearly a quarter of respondents reported no conservation knowledge highlights gaps in awareness. Strengthening community-driven strategies, including funding for medicinal plant management [45], secures both livelihood benefits and biodiversity conservation. Based on the respondents’ perceptions and the limitations of the present study, we propose several complementary priorities for future management. First, ecological inventories and population monitoring are needed to determine whether perceived local scarcity corresponds to measurable differences in abundance, regeneration or population structure. Second, studies of harvesting intensity and plant responses are necessary to evaluate the sustainability of leaf collection. Third, cultivation and agroforestry integration could be investigated as potential complementary strategies for reducing dependence on wild populations. Ex situ approaches could also complement in situ conservation and sustainable harvesting. Depending on the reproductive biology and seed storage behavior of the species, these approaches could include seed banking, living collections, propagation programs and the conservation of plant tissues for future restoration or cultivation. Such measures should complement, rather than replace, the conservation of natural habitats and wild populations.

sec.title: 4.4. Limitations of the Study
sec.p: This study provides a broad ethnobotanical assessment of Pavetta crassipes across Benin; however, several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, information on uses, availability, threats and conservation measures were self-reported and may be influenced by recall bias, differences in individual experience or respondents’ willingness to disclose information. Second, perceived availability and observations regarding developmental stages were not validated through standardized ecological inventories, population assessments or long-term monitoring. Consequently, the results cannot be used as direct evidence of population decline, demographic change or conservation status at the local level. Third, the study did not quantify harvesting frequency, quantities collected, seasonality or harvesting techniques. Therefore, although leaves were the most frequently reported plant part, the ecological consequences of leaf harvesting could not be evaluated. Fourth, because the survey design focused on communities and markets where knowledge or use of the species was known to occur, the findings should not be interpreted as an unbiased estimate of ethnobotanical knowledge across the entire national population. Finally, the cross-sectional design provides a snapshot of current knowledge and perceptions and does not allow direct evaluation of temporal changes in either local knowledge or population abundance. Despite these limitations, the study provides a national-scale baseline on the reported uses, perceptions and management perspectives surrounding P. crassipes. Future research combining ethnobotanical surveys with ecological inventories, demographic monitoring and quantitative assessments of harvesting practices will be necessary to evaluate the relationship between human use and population dynamics.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: This study provides a broad-scale assessment across Benin of the ethnobotanical importance, reported uses and perceived availability of Pavetta crassipes in Benin. Respondents reported a wide range of medicinal applications, with leaves being the most frequently cited plant part and malaria among the most commonly reported health conditions treated with the species. Respondents also reported seasonal constraints in access to the species and identified bushfires, commercialization and harvesting practices as major perceived pressures. However, because the study did not include ecological inventories, population assessments or temporal monitoring, these perceptions should not be interpreted as direct evidence of population decline or changes in local conservation status. Similarly, although leaf harvesting was the predominant form of plant-part use, its sustainability cannot be assessed without quantitative information on harvesting frequency, quantities removed and plant responses. Nevertheless, the findings nevertheless provide an important baseline for guiding future ecological and conservation research on P. crassipes. Integrating local knowledge with systematic ecological monitoring will be essential to determine whether perceived changes in species availability correspond to measurable changes abundance, population structure regeneration or habitat distribution. Future research should prioritized geographical comparisons of species availability and harvesting intensity, on plant performance and regeneration, the development of sustainable harvesting guidelines and evaluation of cultivation and agroforestry options. Ex situ conservation approaches, including seed banking, living collections, and propagation programs, may further complement in situ conservation where biologically and technically appropriate.

No personally identifiable information was collected or used in the analyses or reporting of the findings.
